definition: The AI effect is a phenomenon in which advances in artificial intelligence lead to a redefinition of what is considered intelligence, such that capabilities achieved by AI systems are no longer regarded as examples of "real" intelligence.
details: The concept has been used to describe both a cognitive tendency and a sociotechnical pattern, in which successful AI techniques are reclassified as routine computation or absorbed into other domains. Historian Pamela McCorduck described this as a recurring feature of AI research, noting in her 2004 book Machines Who Think that once a problem is solved, it is no longer considered evidence of intelligence. Researcher Rodney Brooks similarly observed in 2002 that once systems are understood, they are often regarded as "just computation".

explainer.lead: The AI effect is the tendency to stop calling a machine capability intelligent once it works reliably and we understand how it does it. It matters because yesterday’s remarkable AI achievement can become today’s ordinary software, making progress in artificial intelligence easy to overlook.

tiers.eli5: Imagine being amazed by a magic trick until someone explains it, and then saying, “That’s not magic—it’s just a trick.” People can do the same with computers: once a machine learns to play chess or understand speech, they may call it ordinary calculation instead of intelligence. The goalposts for what counts as “real” intelligence keep moving.
tiers.practitioner: The AI effect is useful as a lens when explaining deployed systems: capabilities such as speech recognition or optical character recognition may be treated as routine engineering rather than AI once they become reliable. It also appears in discussions of large language models, where understood behavior may be described as statistical or mechanical. A pitfall is assuming either that reclassification proves a system has no intelligence or that the AI label alone establishes genuine understanding.
tiers.paperLevel: The AI effect can be expressed as: if capability C was previously treated as evidence of intelligence, successful automation and understanding of C often lead to its reclassification as routine computation. McCorduck described successful techniques being absorbed into other domains, while Brooks observed that understood systems are often regarded as “just computation”; Tesler’s theorem summarizes the pattern as “AI is whatever hasn’t been done yet.” Interpretations include cognitive bias, sociotechnical normalization, and genuine philosophical distinctions, so the phenomenon alone does not settle what intelligence is.

explainer.example: IBM’s Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov in 1997. Although chess playing had been regarded as a demonstration of machine intelligence, critics argued that Deep Blue relied on brute-force methods rather than genuine understanding, illustrating how the achievement could be reclassified after success.

usedIn.name: Game playing
usedIn.detail: Checkers and chess achievements were reinterpreted as computation as the systems improved and became better understood.

usedIn.name: Optical character recognition
usedIn.detail: Once a core AI problem, it came to be treated as a standard engineering solution as reliability and deployment increased.

usedIn.name: Speech recognition
usedIn.detail: Its successful automation illustrates how a former indicator of intelligence can become routine technology.

usedIn.name: Generative AI
usedIn.detail: Large language model capabilities are sometimes described as statistical or mechanical once they are understood.

explainer.intuition: People often reserve “intelligence” for abilities machines have not yet mastered. When a machine succeeds, the achievement can be redefined as mere calculation, while AI research moves on to the remaining unsolved problems.
howItWorks: A task such as chess or speech recognition is treated as evidence of intelligence.
An AI system learns to perform the task successfully.
The system’s methods become better understood or widely deployed.
The capability is relabeled as computation, engineering, or part of another field.
Expectations shift toward capabilities that remain unsolved.
explainer.whyItMatters: The AI effect shapes how research progress is recognized, named, and absorbed into everyday applications. It also exposes a deeper disagreement: reclassification may reflect shifting expectations, commercial normalization, or meaningful distinctions about the nature of intelligence.
misconceptions: It does not mean that AI research has made no progress.
Reclassifying a technology does not by itself prove whether it involves intelligence.
The effect is not only individual bias; technologies can also lose the AI label as they spread and succeed commercially.
